passage: Come, have some tea. I will tell you about my second team, the one that never had a fight about work. I am Elizabeth, and back then I led five people. In our very first week we stood at a whiteboard and asked each other: what is fair? Kunal, the youngest, said he could do late testing but not weekends because of his night classes. Someone else said she preferred writing. We agreed on hours, wrote our names next to tasks, and put a tick when each one was done. Every Friday we looked at the board for five minutes. When Kunal's column looked light one week, he said so first, and we moved a task. Nobody was blamed.

qa.q: What did the team do in their very first week?
qa.a: In their very first week they stood at a whiteboard and asked each other what is fair.

qa.q: What might Kunal have felt when saying first that the column looked light?
qa.a: Kunal probably felt a little nervous but safe enough to be honest, since the team had already agreed openly on what fair looked like and nobody was blamed.

qa.q: What simple habit kept the team from resentment?
qa.a: They wrote names next to tasks, ticked them off, and looked at the board together every Friday for five minutes.

qa.q: What was it like for Kunal to work under the agreed hours because of the night classes?
qa.a: Kunal could do late testing but not weekends, and having that spoken openly meant the limit was accepted rather than hidden as a reason for guilt.

grounding: A team agrees openly what fair effort looks like and tracks it simply, so fairness discussed early avoids resentment later, told by an elder.

passage: Two days before the product launch, Sarika gathered the team of five in the only room with lights, since a power cut had knocked out the rest of the office. "Before we split anything, what does fair effort mean for us?" she asked. Gargi said she could not do nights but could start at six in the morning. Ashok said he wanted a say in who takes the tedious jobs. Nobody dissented; even quiet Ravi murmured, "Let us write it down." On a torn flip-chart page they wrote names, tasks and hours, and drew boxes to tick. By the morning of the launch there were no grudges, only ticks.

qa.q: Why was the team gathered in the only room with lights?
qa.a: A power cut had knocked out the rest of the office.

qa.q: Why does Sarika ask what fair effort means before splitting the work?
qa.a: Sarika wants agreement on fairness before resentment can build; even under time pressure she sees this as protecting the team.

qa.q: What made the agreement easy to follow during the launch rush?
qa.a: They wrote names, tasks and hours on one page and drew tick boxes, so everyone could see who owed what without arguing.

qa.q: What might Ravi be feeling when murmuring "Let us write it down"?
qa.a: Ravi probably feels relieved that a fair and visible plan is forming; being quiet, the written page gives a safe way to have a say.

grounding: A team agrees openly what fair effort looks like and tracks it simply, avoiding slow-burning resentment later, even under time pressure.

passage:
The four new flatmates in the Indiranagar flat sat on the floor with pizza on their first Sunday. Avni pulled out a notebook.
“Before anything goes wrong,” she said, “let's decide what fair means. Cooking, cleaning, bills, groceries.”
Arnab groaned. “We're adults. It'll work out.”
“That's what my last flat said,” Avni replied. “By month three, two people weren't speaking.”
They agreed: each person picks two chores a week, marks a tick on the fridge chart. If anyone falls behind, they say so before someone else notices.
A month later, Arnab had four ticks missing. On Sunday he said, “My exams. Can I do extra next week?” Nobody sulked. They just nodded.

qa.q: Where did the flatmates stick the chart?
qa.a: On the fridge.

qa.q: How did the flatmates feel when Arnab fell behind?
qa.a: They felt calm and accepting, not resentful, because the rule for falling behind had been agreed early.

qa.q: Why did Avni's early conversation help?
qa.a: Agreeing on fair effort and a simple tick chart at the start meant problems were raised openly before resentment built up.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt admitting the missed ticks?
qa.a: He might have felt a little embarrassed but relieved that the agreed rule let him ask for a swap without a fight.

grounding: Shows a group agreeing early and openly what fair effort looks like and tracking it simply, which prevents resentment.

passage:
“Before we start the app project,” Nazia said, “can we agree what fair looks like?”
Tanvir laughed. “Fair is everyone does their bit.”
“And what's a bit?” Nazia asked. “Last project, Rohan did twice what Priyam did and nobody said anything until the launch party.”
Priyam winced. “Fair point.”
“So,” Nazia went on, “we each take one feature. We post a one-line update every Friday. If someone's stuck, they say it on Friday, not the night before.”
“And if someone's slacking?”
“Then we talk to them that same Friday. Kindly.”
Tanvir shrugged. “Okay. Put it on the board.”
Nazia wrote it in big letters. Everyone signed their initials underneath.

qa.q: When would the team post their updates?
qa.a: They would post a one-line update every Friday.

qa.q: How did Priyam seem to feel when Nazia mentioned the last project?
qa.a: Priyam seemed embarrassed, wincing, but agreed it was a fair point.

qa.q: What does the team's agreement do well?
qa.a: It defines fair effort clearly, tracks it simply with Friday updates, and sets a kind way to raise slacking early.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see the agreement at first?
qa.a: Tanvir seemed to think it was unnecessary, but shrugged and accepted it once it was simple and clear.

grounding: Shows a team agreeing openly what fair effort means and tracking it simply, to avoid slow resentment later.

passage:
I'm Ritu, and I've been volunteering at the community kitchen for three years. The first year nearly broke us.
There were twelve of us. Some came every Sunday at six to chop vegetables. Some came at noon, served for twenty minutes, and took photos. By winter, Madhuri and I were barely speaking to the photo crowd. Nobody had said anything out loud, but everyone was angry.
In the second year, Madhuri suggested a meeting before we started. We agreed: everyone does at least one prep shift a month, and we write names on a simple sheet by the door.
Some people left. Most stayed. The anger never came back. I think it was never about the work. It was about nobody saying what fair meant.

qa.q: What time did some volunteers come to chop vegetables?
qa.a: They came every Sunday at six.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel about the photo crowd in the first year?
qa.a: Ritu felt angry and resentful, barely speaking to them, though nobody said anything out loud.

qa.q: Which change worked, and why?
qa.a: Agreeing early on one prep shift a month with names on a sheet made fair effort clear and visible, so anger didn't build.

qa.q: How might the volunteers who left have seen the new rule?
qa.a: They may have felt it asked more than they wanted to give, and chose to go rather than change.

grounding: A volunteer recalls how agreeing openly on fair effort and tracking it simply ended a year of slow-burning resentment.

passage:
Team coach's note, week 3 of the app redesign.
Before work began, Sachin put a blank sheet on the wall and said, "On the last project, three of us were angry by week six and nobody said so. Let's decide now what fair looks like."
Vaibhav suggested each person take two tickets a week and flag early if they'll miss one. Nidhi added that design reviews count as work too, which nobody had thought of. Kabir asked what happens if someone's ill; they agreed the team reshuffles, no blame. The tracker is a column of names and ticks.
Three weeks in, Kabir flagged a missed ticket on Tuesday, not Friday, and Nidhi picked it up without a sigh. Stand-ups are calmer than anything I've seen on this floor all year.
What I did next: I asked Sachin to show the sheet to the other two teams.

qa.q: How many tickets a week did Vaibhav suggest each person take?
qa.a: Two tickets a week.

qa.q: What feeling seems to push Sachin to start the discussion?
qa.a: Sachin seems wary and a little tired of old resentment, remembering three people angry and silent by week six last time.

qa.q: Why does agreeing on fairness before the work starts help?
qa.a: Everyone knows the rules in advance, so a missed ticket is flagged early and handled by agreement instead of building quiet anger.

qa.q: How might Nidhi experience covering Kabir's missed ticket?
qa.a: Nidhi seems calm about it, probably because the rule was agreed openly and it doesn't feel like being taken advantage of 🙂

grounding: Shows a team openly agreeing what fair effort means at the start and tracking it simply, which prevents slow-building resentment.
